tasks.q: Count down to 1 with a while loop, then print go.
brief: Read one whole number.
Print every number from it down to 1, one on each line.
Then print: go
tasks.starter: # Count down to 1, then print go

tests.why: Counting down means the number gets smaller each time round. If your numbers went up instead, you added 1 where you should have taken 1 away.
With 1 the loop should run exactly once. Printing go before the number means your print is in the wrong place.
With 0 the condition is false straight away, so the loop body never runs. If you printed a 0 here you have used a loop that always runs at least once.
If this one never finished, you forgot to change n inside the loop - the condition stays true for ever.

tasks.fb: A while loop tests its condition before each go, so it can run zero times. Change the variable the condition uses inside the loop, or the loop never ends.

teach.say: A while loop keeps going while its condition is true. Change the variable the condition uses inside the loop, or it never stops.

tasks.q: Count how many doublings it takes to reach a target.
brief: Read one whole number: the target.
Start at 1 and keep doubling until the target is reached.
Print only how many doublings that took.
tasks.starter: # Double until the target is reached, then print the number of doublings

tests.why: 1 doubles to 2, then 4, then 8 - that is 3 weeks. A 4 here means you stopped one week early, before the target was actually reached.
The weed already covers 1 square metre, so no weeks are needed. If you printed 1 you used a loop that always runs once instead of testing the condition first.
After 2 weeks the weed covers 4, which is not yet 5, so a third week is needed. The loop stops when the area is reached or passed, not only when it matches exactly.
The sizes go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. A program that only worked for small numbers will be wrong here.

tasks.fb: This is a condition-controlled loop: you cannot know the number of weeks in advance, so while is the right choice and for is not.

teach.say: You cannot know in advance how many turns this takes, so a while loop is the right choice. Keep a separate variable to count the turns.

tasks.q: Keep asking until a number from 1 to 20 is typed.
brief: Read whole numbers until one is from 1 to 20.
Print: out of range - for each number that is refused.
Then print the word locker, a space, and the accepted number.
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the number is from 1 to 20

tests.why: The first number is already valid, so nothing should be printed about the range. If you printed out of range here, your check runs before the loop condition, or you used a loop that always runs once.
Two bad numbers means two warnings. If you only got one, you used an if instead of a while - an if checks once and then gives up.
20 is inside the range. Rejecting it means you wrote n > 19 or n >= 20 where you needed n > 20.
21 is just outside and 1 is the bottom boundary. Getting this wrong usually means a < where a <= was needed, or the other way round.

tasks.fb: The shape is: read once, then while the value is still wrong, warn and read again. Putting the read inside the loop as well as before it is what lets the loop run zero times.

teach.say: Read once before the loop. Then, while the value is still wrong, warn and read again.

tasks.q: Keep asking until the answer is yes or no.
brief: Read words until one of them is yes or no.
Print: please answer yes or no - for each other word.
Then print the word accepted, a space, and the word given.
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the answer is yes or no

tests.why: no is already a valid answer, so the loop must not run at all. A warning here means your loop body runs before the condition is tested.
Both yes and no are accepted. If only one of them works, your condition tests for a single word instead of ruling out both.
Two wrong answers, so two warnings. One warning only means an if was used where a while was needed.
y is not the word yes, so it must be rejected. Comparing only the first letter accepts things the brief says to refuse.

tasks.fb: Two words are allowed, so the condition has to rule out both: use and, not or. 'not yes or not no' is always true and gives an endless loop.

teach.say: Two answers are allowed, so the condition has to rule out both of them with and.

tasks.q: Total the numbers typed in, stopping at -1.
brief: Read whole numbers until -1 is typed.
The -1 is the signal to stop, not a number to add.
Print only the total.
tasks.starter: # Add up the numbers until -1 stops you

tests.why: The three prices add up to 250. A 249 means you added the -1 as well - the signal value is not data.
The shopper bought nothing, so the total is 0. A crash here means you read a second number after the -1; the loop must test before it reads again.
One price only. Check your total starts at 0 before the loop, not at the first price.
Four prices, however many there are. A program that handles a fixed number of prices will fail here.

tasks.fb: A sentinel is a value that cannot be real data and means stop. Read one value before the loop, add it inside, then read the next at the end of the body.

teach.say: Read one value before the loop. Use it inside the loop, then read the next one at the bottom of the loop.

tasks.q: Print the highest number typed in before the word end.
brief: Read lines until the word end is read.
Print the highest number that was read.
If end is the very first line, print: no readings
tasks.starter: # Read numbers until the word end, then print the highest

tests.why: 21 is the biggest. A 19 here means you printed the last reading rather than keeping the best one so far.
The loop runs zero times, so there is nothing to compare. A crash means you tried int() on the word end - read the line as text first, then convert it only once you know it is not the sentinel.
With one reading, that reading is the highest.
All the readings are below zero. A 0 here means you started your highest at 0, so no real reading could ever beat it. Start from the first reading instead.

tasks.fb: Never start a highest-so-far at 0 - a reading below zero can never beat it. Start it from the first value you read, or mark it as not set yet.

teach.say: A sentinel can be a word, so read the line as text and only turn it into a number once you know it is not the sentinel.

tasks.q: Count the numbers typed before -1, and how many reach 40.
brief: Read whole numbers until -1 is typed.
Print how many numbers were read.
Then print how many of them were 40 or more.
tasks.starter: # Count the numbers, and count how many reach 40

tests.why: Four scores, and 55 and 40 both reach 40. A 5 on the first line means you counted the -1 as a score.
No scores at all, so both counts are 0. Both counters must be set before the loop, so they still have a value when the loop runs zero times.
39 does not reach 40. A 1 on the second line means you wrote > 39 as >= 39, or used > 40 the wrong way round somewhere.
Exactly 40 counts as reaching 40. If you got 1 here, you used > 40 instead of >= 40.

tasks.fb: Two counters, both set to 0 before the loop. One counts every time round, the other only counts when the if is true.

teach.say: Each thing you count needs its own variable, set to 0 before the loop and changed only when it should be.

tasks.q: Add up the digits of a whole number with a while loop.
brief: Read one whole number that is 0 or more.
Add up its digits without turning it into text.
Print only the total of the digits.
tasks.starter: # Take the last digit off the number each time round

tests.why: 4 + 7 + 2 is 13. A 2 here means your loop only went round once - check you divide the number down inside the loop as well as taking the last digit off.
0 has no digits left to take off, so the loop runs zero times and the total is still 0. A crash or no output means your total was never set before the loop.
A single digit. Getting 0 here means your condition stopped the loop before the last digit was used.
Only the 1 counts; the zeros add nothing. If this one never finished, your division used / instead of //, so the number never reaches 0 exactly.
Five nines make 45. A program that only looked at two or three digits will be short here.

tasks.fb: n % 10 gives the last digit and n // 10 removes it. Using / instead of // leaves a decimal, the condition never becomes false and the loop runs for ever.

teach.say: n % 10 gives the last digit and n // 10 takes it off. // keeps the answer whole, so the number can reach 0 exactly.

tasks.q: Read the parcels with a for loop, then check limits with while.
brief: Read how many parcels there are, then that many weights.
Read a limit; while it is below the heaviest parcel, print: limit too low - and read another.
When a limit is accepted, print: ok
tasks.starter: # A for loop for the parcels, a while loop for the limit

tests.why: The heaviest parcel is 25 and the limit is 30, so the while loop runs zero times. A warning here means you compared the limit with the last parcel rather than the heaviest.
Two limits are refused before one is accepted. One warning only means you used an if where a while was needed.
With 0 parcels the for loop runs zero times, so no weights are read and the first limit is accepted. A crash means your loop read a weight anyway.
A limit equal to the heaviest parcel is allowed. Refusing it means you used <= where < was needed.
Two parcels of the same weight, then one refused limit. If this went wrong, check you only read one limit per go round the while loop.

tasks.fb: Use for when the number of repeats is known before you start, and while when it depends on what the user does next. This question needs one of each.

teach.say: Use for when you know how many turns there will be, and while when it depends on what the user types next. One program can use both.

tasks.q: Give a higher or lower hint until 37 is guessed.
brief: The secret number is 37.
While the guess is wrong, print: higher - or: lower - then read another guess.
Once 37 is guessed, print: correct
tasks.starter: # The secret is 37. Hint at every wrong guess.

tests.why: The first guess is right, so no hint should appear at all. A hint here means your loop body runs before the condition is tested.
10 is too low so the answer is higher; 50 is too high so it is lower. Swapping these two means you read the hint as what the guess was, not what the player should try next.
Two guesses just above the secret. If this one never finished, you printed the hint but forgot to read a new guess inside the loop.
36 is one below, so the player should go higher. An off-by-one here usually means you compared with <= 37 instead of < 37.

tasks.fb: The condition tests only whether the guess is right; the if inside the loop chooses the hint. Reading the next guess must be inside the loop, or it never changes.

teach.say: The condition tests only whether the guess is right. An if inside the loop chooses which hint to give.

tasks.q: Print how many swims there were, the total and the longest.
brief: Read whole numbers until the word close is read.
Print how many there were, then the total, then the longest.
If close is the very first line, print only: no swimmers
tasks.starter: # Count the swims, total the minutes, remember the longest

tests.why: Three swims adding to 95, the longest being 45. A 20 on the last line means you printed the final swim instead of the longest one.
The loop runs zero times, so there is nothing to report. Printing three zeros means you skipped the check for an empty session; a crash means you converted close to a number.
With one swimmer the total and the longest swim are the same number as the swim itself.
Four equal swims. A 1 on the first line means you only counted values you had not seen before, instead of counting every line.
The longest swim is in the middle, not at either end, so a program that only checked the first or last value will be wrong.

tasks.fb: One pass through the data can keep a count, a running total and a best-so-far at the same time. Set all three before the loop, so the empty session still has sensible values to test.

teach.say: A best-so-far is set up before the loop and replaced only when a bigger value turns up.

tasks.q: Which kind of loop does each job need?
items: Ask until a valid locker number is typed
Keep guessing until the number is right
Add up a known number of marks
Double the weed until it covers the pond
tasks.fb: If you can say the number of repeats before the loop starts, use for.

info.title: Stuck forever
info.text: If a program stops responding, an infinite loop is often why: the condition it waits for can never become False.

info.title: Ask again politely
info.text: A good validation loop says what was wrong with the last answer, not just 'try again'.

info.title: Choosing a sentinel
info.text: -1 works for a price, because a price can never be negative. For a temperature it would be a terrible choice.

info.title: Count or total
info.text: A counter always adds 1. A running total adds whatever came in. Plenty of programs need both at once.

info.title: Testing at the bottom
info.text: Some languages have a loop that tests its condition at the end, so it always runs once. Python does not, so the first read goes above the loop.

info.title: No data at all
info.text: A program given no data should still print something sensible. Start every total at zero and it will.
